person.name: Gattu Rithvik
person.line: Third-year IT student in Hyderabad. I build LLM tools and write down what broke.
person.tagline: Curiosity to ideas. Ideas to products.
person.college: B.Tech in Information Technology, Vardhaman College of Engineering

about: I’m a third-year IT student at Vardhaman College of Engineering in Hyderabad. I’ve done ten-plus hackathons, and most of what’s on this page came out of one.
I like LLM tooling that has to be reliable: prompt testing, agents that explain their decisions, retrieval that cites its sources. I’m less interested in demos that only work once.

I write down what broke. The ticket above is built that way. Every project has a line about what went wrong, because those lines are where I learned something. I also keep a few short essays on building. The one I keep coming back to: an interesting idea isn’t always a useful one.

ticket.title: Hackathon season 2026
ticket.hint: Scratch the ticket. Each panel is something I built. One is hiding.

projects.title: PromptShield CI
projects.what: Safety and regression checks for LLM prompts, run in CI before a prompt ships.

projects.title: POINT.FEEDBACK
projects.what: On-screen feedback tool. You point at something on a page and your annotation becomes a developer ticket.

projects.title: OpsBrain AI
projects.what: Knowledge copilot for industrial documents. It gives cited answers, flags compliance gaps, and surfaces patterns across past incidents.
projects.wrong: The demo corpus is seven documents. It works end to end, but it isn’t hardened, and I know it.

projects.title: Payment Recovery Agent
projects.what: Agent that works out why a subscription payment failed and picks what to do next: retry, offer a discount, send an update link, or escalate to a person.
projects.wrong: A multi-cycle simulation showed over a third of a seeded batch stuck in pending_retry forever. Nothing requeued it, and the retry delays in the config weren’t used anywhere. Fixed, and the delays are real now.

projects.title: Déjà Vu
projects.what: Reviews a deploy or config change and answers SHIP, REVIEW or HOLD from the team’s own history. It learns when an engineer overrules it, and marks old lessons stale.
projects.wrong: The 65% drop in wrong calls comes from a simulated benchmark with a scripted oracle. It shows the mechanism works. It doesn’t show real-world accuracy.

projects.title: ripple
projects.what: CLI that reads git history, finds files that usually change together, and warns you when one is missing from your diff.
projects.wrong: I benchmarked it on the newest 100 commits of three small Python repos: itsdangerous, click and markupsafe. That’s a small sample.

projects.title: ClausePilot
projects.event: Hack2skill: AI for Legal Assistance and Access
projects.what: Reads a freelance contract, compares each clause with standard ones, flags the risky ones, and drafts counter-messages plus a prep sheet for talking to a lawyer.
projects.wrong: The live demo ran through a Cloudflare tunnel from my laptop. Fine for a demo, not a deployment.

projects.title: TenderWin AI
projects.what: Multi-agent system for answering RFPs. A writer agent drafts each answer and a critic agent reviews it.

projects.title: Keyframe
projects.what: Keeps a structured project state across AI chat sessions, writes handoff prompts, and checks new AI-written code against decisions you made earlier.
projects.wrong: I restarted the build from scratch and cut the backend and the database. Everything lives in localStorage now.

projects.title: Unilog enrichment pipeline
projects.what: Turns messy product catalog rows (six input columns) into a structured product record with 252 columns.
projects.wrong: I only had three files. The reference tables the solution guide depends on, such as content guidelines, units and the brand master list, were missing.

projects.title: FlowSync, the one I shelved
projects.what: Started as a Hyderabad traffic-routing demo. I turned it into an energy-corridor risk tool: live news signals, a scenario modeller for refinery run-rates and fuel prices, and a ranking engine for procurement options.
projects.wrong: I built two projects for the same hackathon and had to pick one. OpsBrain went forward, FlowSync didn’t. Along the way the Gemini key went invalid so I switched to Groq, Google Maps billing blocked me so I hardcoded the corridors, and Cloudflare returned a 403 on my Python requests until I switched to httpx. A route screen from the old traffic app also had to go, because point-to-point routing makes no sense for shipping corridors.
